name: PT Aspirasi Hidup Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Aspirasi Hidup Indonesia: the rebrand is paid for, the cash flow is not
frontmatter.summary: ACES has re-based margins after losing the ACE Hardware licence, and the market still prices a decline. We think the reset is finished: nine-month sales grew faster than the retail market, the payout ratio is at a record, and the shares trade near book with net cash. BUY.
thesis: The post-rebrand margin reset is already in the numbers; we forecast the delivered operating margin, not a recovery to the pre-2025 level.
Nine-month 2026 sales grew well ahead of a contracting retail market, with positive same-store sales, which says the AZKO and NEKA formats are holding share.
The company pays out the bulk of its earnings, holds net cash, and trades at a low multiple of the cash it actually generates.

The principal risk is ACE Hardware under MAP taking the branded end of the category; our bear case models that share loss, a gross margin below the delivered level, the loss of the below-the-line income and a dividend cut, and even then the value is above today's price.

The rating rests on the base-case cash flow, not on the bear row of the scenario table. The DCF carries most of the weight and is re-priced in every scenario, while the two earnings multiples are applied to trailing metrics the model does not re-base, which we disclose rather than bury.

catalysts.event: FY2026 results and the fourth-quarter trading update
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration
Further ACE Hardware store openings under MAP in Jakarta and Serpong
Bank Indonesia retail sales survey for the year-end trading period

blocks.text: **BUY, target Rp631, 91.6% total return** from Rp348 including the forward dividend. ACES is the Indonesian home-improvement and household-goods retailer that spent twenty-nine years as the ACE Hardware licensee, lost that licence at the end of 2024, and re-branded its big-box network as AZKO while launching a smaller value format, NEKA [S6, S11]. The market has treated the break as permanent damage: the shares sit at 7.7x forward earnings, 3.5x EV/EBITDA and 0.9x book, having de-rated from roughly sixteen times earnings two years ago [S0].
Our view is that the damage is real but already paid for, and that the price now discounts a decline that the delivered numbers do not show. Three things carry the call.

**First, the trading is ahead of the market, not behind it.** Nine-month sales were 6,900 billion rupiah, and the reported growth of 8.3 per cent compares with a Bank Indonesia retail index that grew 0.6 per cent in September [S2, S15]. Same-store sales grew 2.4 per cent, which is the part that matters: a retailer adding stores can always print revenue growth, but positive same-store sales on a network that has just been re-branded says the customer did not leave with the licence [S2].

**Second, our forecasts do not need the margin to recover.** The operating margin fell from 11.9% in FY2024 to 7.2% in FY2025 and has run at about that level through the first nine months of 2026 [S0]. We hold it there and take only a small amount of operating leverage over five years. Anyone waiting for the old margin is waiting for something we are not paying for.

**Third, the cash is real and most of it comes back.** The FY2025 dividend was 548 billion rupiah, 32.01 rupiah a share and 82 per cent of earnings, the highest payout ratio the company has paid, and the shares yield 10.3% on our forward estimate [S13]. The balance sheet carried net cash at the last year end and still does at the third quarter [S0].

What does the price imply? Our reverse-DCF solver is not usable here and we say so plainly: its only lever is revenue growth, and in a model where capital expenditure and working capital scale with the change in revenue, slower growth mechanically raises free cash flow, so the solver cannot reproduce Rp348 at any growth rate and the answer tells us nothing about the market. The informative read is in the valuation section: at today's price the cash flows we forecast are discounted at a rate far above our cost of capital, or our free cash flow is roughly halved and stays there. That is the bet: not that ACES returns to its old multiple, but that a business earning 12.3% of free cash flow to equity on today's price, rising to 15.9% by FY2028E, stops being priced for extinction.

**What the target is, and what the rating rests on.** The target above is the probability-weighted blend of a discounted cash flow, a P/E leg and an EV/EBITDA leg, and it sits below the DCF value of Rp658 because both multiples come out below the cash flow. The scenario machinery re-prices the model's own inputs, which means the DCF moves in every case while the two earnings legs — applied to trailing metrics from the data pack — do not. That flatters the bear row of the scenario table and understates the bull, and the scenario section says so beside the numbers. We do not publish a hand-recomputed alternative to the target: every figure here is taken from the model, and a number typed by hand could not be traced back to it. What the rating rests on is the cash flow leg, which carries most of the weight and is the only one the scenarios re-price, plus the base case at Rp628; and a bear case with its earnings legs cut to what its own earnings would support still leaves the shares above Rp348. For the reader who wants to reconcile the two, the correction is small at the target level and large in the bear row: marking each case's multiples to its own earnings leaves the weighted value a few per cent below the printed target and the bear row roughly a third above the value the downside actually supports. The correction reduces the expected return; it does not change the rating.

The Indonesian modern-retail trade has spent a decade consolidating around a handful of listed
operators, and the market has repeatedly marked the premium names down when a licence, a format or a
supplier relationship changed hands. The pattern to watch is not the first year of a re-brand but the
third, when the store fleet has been refreshed, the new formats have opened, and the customer either
followed the brand or did not.

PT Aspirasi Hidup Indonesia Tbk, which trades as ACES and was formerly PT Ace Hardware Indonesia, is a multi-brand retailer of home-improvement, household and lifestyle products [S0]. Its formats are AZKO, the large-format hardware and home-improvement chain that replaced the ACE Hardware banner; NEKA, a smaller value-oriented household format launched in 2025; ATARU and Pendopo, lifestyle and home accents; and Toys Kingdom, which sits in a subsidiary [S2, S14]. It also sells online through ruparupa [S0].

The operating model is a leasehold big-box and mall network buying imported and locally sourced hardware, housewares and lifestyle goods, and selling them at a gross margin near 47.6% [S0]. The merchandise is broad and deep rather than fashion-driven, which is why the inventory line is the dominant asset on the balance sheet and why gross margin is stable across the cycle. The company reports its merchandise across home-improvement products, lifestyle products and toys, without disclosing a revenue split by category [S0]; we therefore do not rank the three, and the forecasts are built on the total sales line rather than a category mix.

**The licence event is the company's history.** ACES operated the ACE Hardware brand in Indonesia for twenty-nine years; that agreement ended at the end of 2024, and the company re-badged the network as AZKO through 2025 [S6]. The principal then appointed PT Mitra Adiperkasa Tbk, the MAP group, as its new Indonesian partner, and MAP opened its first ACE Hardware store at Sunter Mall in Jakarta at the end of July 2026, with a second in Serpong to follow [S9]. Management's own framing is that the returning brand is now "a choice for the public" and that AZKO competes on product, price, people, after-sales service and store reach [S6].

**Footprint and strategy.** At the end of 2025 the AZKO network was 265 stores in ninety cities, of which the majority are on Java and the balance outside it [S11]. By September 2026 it was 282 stores, and NEKA had reached 31 stores having opened 10 of them in 2025 [S2, S11]. The stated strategy is to keep opening in tier-two and tier-three cities, to scale NEKA in the value segment, and to rejuvenate existing AZKO stores rather than only add new ones [S11, S14]. Management guided to 30 AZKO openings in the high case and up to 50 NEKA openings for 2026 [S7, S11].

**What NEKA is worth and why it is not a separate line in our model.** NEKA is a small-format mass-market household store, capped at 700 square metres, focused on suburban and tier-two and tier-three locations and, on management's own account, faster to roll out and cheaper per store in capex than AZKO [S10]. That makes the format's economics different in kind from the big box: lower sales per store, lower fit-out cost, and a shorter payback. The company does not disclose NEKA revenue, sales per store or format capex, and we will not invent them; what we can say is that 31 stores averaging below the AZKO box cannot yet carry a material share of a IDR9,277.9bn sales base, so NEKA is inside our consolidated growth and margin rather than a separate valuation. Its value to the case is optionality and mix: it is the format that competes where the returning ACE Hardware brand does not, and it is the reason the store programme can continue at a capex budget below the announced range. The bear case gives it no credit; the bull case lets its mix effect hold gross margin rather than dilute it.

**Group and control.** ACES is part of the Kawan Lama Group, the family-owned Indonesian retail and industrial group that founded the business [S6, S14]. The holdings file attributes 61.4% of the shares to insiders and 9.8% to institutions on its own classification, while the exchange's free-float figure is 39.7%; the two come from different registers and do not sum, so we quote each on its own basis rather than derive a float arithmetically [S0]. The company is a subsidiary of the group rather than the group itself, so the listed vehicle owns the retail formats and the brand, and the property and industrial businesses sit outside it; that structure is the source of the related-party question we return to in the governance section.

**What kind of business this is.** ACES is a leader in a category it created, with a store density and an after-sales network that no challenger can replicate quickly, and it is now a challenger to its own former brand [S6, S11]. It is not a growth company: the store base is large relative to the addressable modern-trade wallet, and the economics come from merchandise margin, inventory turns and cost control rather than from new square metres. That is the frame for everything that follows.

**The market is weak and getting weaker.** Bank Indonesia's retail sales survey — the reference series for modern-trade demand — grew 0.6 per cent year on year in September 2026, down from the prior month's pace, and contracted month on month after independence-day demand normalised [S15, S16]. The categories that held up were vehicle parts and accessories and the residual "other" group, which is the closest read-across to a hardware and household retailer; food, beverage and tobacco and vehicle fuel were the drags [S16]. This is a purchasing-power story, not a retail-specific one: the firm's own macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with the rupiah under strain, which squeezes the imported share of a hardware assortment [S0, S15].

Against that, ACES grew sales faster than the index. The company attributes it to existing-store productivity, operating efficiency and community-based marketing, with Jakarta and the outer islands outperforming and Java outside Jakarta flat [S2, S14]. We treat the gap between the company's growth and the index as evidence of share gain and store additions, but not as proof that the category is growing, and our forecasts fade the growth accordingly.

**Competitive structure.** The category has three kinds of competitor. The first is the branded hardware chain: ACE Hardware under MAP, which re-entered in 2026 with the principal's brand, the supplier relationships that come with it, and a mall-based rollout in Jakarta and Serpong [S9]. This is the competitor that matters, because it is the same proposition ACES used to own and it competes for the same branded-tool and DIY customer. The second is the building-materials and project-supply format, which serves contractors and renovation projects rather than the walk-in householder. The third is the general marketplace and the value formats, including ACES's own NEKA, which compete for the price-sensitive household basket [S11].

**Moat assessment.** ACES's advantages are distribution density — a store in ninety cities, including tier-two and tier-three towns that a new entrant would take years to reach — an after-sales and service capability that management names as a differentiator, and the purchasing scale of a network that buys for the whole country [S6, S11]. Those are real and they are what a new ACE Hardware franchise has to build. What ACES lost with the licence is the brand itself: the principal owns the name, the trade dress and, in a meaningful sense, the customer's mental map of the category. A dense network with a new name is a weaker asset than a dense network with a familiar one, which is precisely why the shares de-rated. Our judgement is that the density and service assets survive the brand loss, but that the pricing power does not fully return; that is why we hold gross margin at the delivered level rather than restoring the FY2024 figure.

**Five forces, briefly.** Supplier power is moderate and rising: a hardware retailer's branded-tool suppliers can choose which Indonesian partner gets the flagship SKUs, and the principal has already demonstrated that it can move a brand. Buyer power is high in the value segment and low in the service-led DIY segment. New entry is hard at the scale of a national network but easy at the level of a single mall store, which is exactly what MAP is doing. Substitutes are the marketplaces and the informal trade. Rivalry is intensifying: the category is not growing in volume, and a well-capitalised entrant has just arrived [S9, S15].

**External influences.** The rupiah is the swing input, because a hardware assortment carries a large imported content and the house macro deck has the currency weakening further; that feeds through cost of goods with a lag and is the main reason we do not forecast gross-margin expansion [S0]. On the demand side, the interest-rate path matters less for a cash-and-carry retailer than for a financed one, but consumer confidence and the subsidy-driven transfer cycle matter a great deal, and both are pointing the wrong way in the current retail survey [S15].

Home-improvement retail sits between two demand pools: discretionary renovation, which moves with
confidence and credit, and repair and maintenance, which moves with the age of the housing stock and is
far stickier. A chain that serves both has a more stable base than its discretionary label suggests,
but it also competes with the informal trade in the smaller towns where its formats are now growing.

**The history is two different companies.** From FY2022 to FY2024 ACES grew sales from IDR6,762.8bn rupiah to IDR8,582.5bn, an increase of roughly a quarter, with the operating margin holding inside a band from 11.0% to 11.9% [S0]. Then FY2025 broke the series: revenue was flat at IDR8,638.7bn, gross margin slipped to 47.6%, and the cost base grew faster than sales, so operating profit fell to IDR623.8bn and earnings per share moved -24.9% [S0]. The cause is the re-brand: a network-wide change of signage, merchandise and systems, a new value format launched from a standing start, and the supplier renegotiation that followed the licence loss, all landing in a year when the sales base did not grow.

**The recovery is in the operating numbers.** Nine-month 2026 sales were 6,900 billion rupiah and attributable profit was 604.7 billion, up about a quarter year on year, with same-store sales of 2.4 per cent and capital expenditure of 144.8 billion against a full-year budget of 400 to 450 billion [S2, S7]. Our FY2026 estimate is revenue of IDR9,277.9bn, operating profit of IDR668.0bn and earnings per share of Rp45, which is the nine months delivered plus a normal fourth quarter, and which reproduces the delivered operating margin of 7.2%.

**The quarterly bridge, because the fourth quarter is where the estimate can hide.** The four-quarter build is simple to state and easy to check against the delivered nine months. Sales of IDR9,277.9bn against the 6,900 billion delivered leaves a fourth quarter of the order of the prior year's peak quarter, which is what a normal seasonal pattern gives [S0, S2]. Profit behaves differently: earnings of IDR768.9bn against the 604.7 billion already delivered leaves a fourth quarter below the prior year's fourth quarter, even though revenue is higher. That is not a margin collapse; it is the below-the-line income excess in the second quarter sitting in the delivered nine months and not being repeated in our fourth-quarter assumption, which is the conservative place to put it. If the fourth quarter repeats the second quarter's excess, the estimate is low and the P/E leg's earnings base is right; if the excess disappears entirely from here, the fourth quarter is still positive and the dividend, not the earnings, is what carries the risk.

**Revenue build.** We grow revenue 7.4% in FY2026E, then 7.0%, 6.0%, 5.5% and 5.0% to FY2030E, with 4.0% in perpetuity. The logic is store-driven: the 2026 plan was 30 AZKO and up to 50 NEKA openings [S7, S11], the new stores are smaller and in lower-density cities, and the FY2025 experience — 27 AZKO openings producing almost no revenue growth — shows how much of a new store's sales is cannibalised from the existing fleet [S0, S11]. Growth therefore sits close to the three-year delivered rate and below nominal GDP.

**The store programme has slipped and we have not pretended otherwise.** The company's own update after the quarter puts the AZKO network at 282 stores at the end of September against 265 at the start of the year and 276 at the half year, with 19 openings counted in the nine months against a plan of up to 30 for the year and only five locations added in the third quarter [S8, S7]. The network is up seventeen net — 19 gross openings less two closures — which is what reconciles 265 at the start of the year to 282 at September; the half-year count of 276 plus the five third-quarter openings falls one short of the September figure, and we treat that single store as a difference in disclosure scope between the half-year and nine-month releases rather than a fact we can resolve. 19 openings against a target of 30, with the last quarter delivering a fraction of what the second quarter did, means five to eleven openings roll into 2027 rather than opening this year. That is small in revenue terms and it is why the growth path is unchanged: the FY2025 cohort added 27 stores for under a point of revenue growth, so a tenth of a percent of sales is the order of the slippage [S0]. We would rather show the reader that arithmetic than quietly trim a forecast by an amount nobody can check.

**Margins and costs.** Gross margin is held at 47.8% and drifts to 47.5% as the value format takes share of the mix. Cost of sales carries imported content and the rupiah path is unhelpful, so we do not model a gross-margin recovery. The cost ratio starts at 40.6% of sales and improves to 39.9%, giving operating margins of 7.2% to 7.6%, a small amount of leverage on a large fixed base and nothing more [S0].

**Cash flow and working capital.** The business converts much of its EBITDA into cash because it leases rather than owns its stores: depreciation and amortisation ran at IDR574.4bn in FY2025 against capital expenditure of IDR187.2bn [S0]. That gap is not free money — the leases sit on the balance sheet as debt and the rent-equivalent is inside the depreciation charge — but it does mean the cash reinvestment requirement is modest and the payout is fundable from operations. Working capital is the constraint: inventory and net working capital absorb 38.3% of sales at a fiscal year end, so every point of growth consumes cash [S0].

The year-end ratio matters, because it carries a large share of the DCF, so we state the choice rather than assert it. Net working capital was IDR3,120.9bn at the FY2025 year end and the ratio was lower there than at the FY2024 year end, when the pre-rebrand assortment was still being carried. We use the average of those two observed year ends, 38.3% of revenue, rather than the better of the two, because the FY2025 figure is a single observation taken in the year the rebrand cut the assortment and the NEKA value format began to change the mix. That is a deliberate step away from the last actual, and it is the conservative end of the evidence rather than the middle of the road. The model's FY2026E year-end working capital is IDR3,553.4bn against IDR3,120.9bn a year earlier, and the cash absorbed in the year is the change between the two year ends, IDR432.5bn [S0]. The September balance sheet shows a higher ratio than either year end because inventory is built through the third quarter for the year-end trade; if that third-quarter level proved structural rather than seasonal, the model would absorb the step and then a larger share of each year's growth. We have run that case: holding the September ratio permanently instead of the two-year average lowers the DCF by about thirty rupiah a share and the target by about twenty, so the call narrows by a few per cent and survives. We hold the average rather than the September level because the two observed December balance sheets are the evidence about December. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR1,248.4bn in FY2025, helped by a working-capital release; we do not capitalise that release, and the model's free cash flow of IDR510.9bn is well below the FY2025 figure for exactly that reason.

**Balance sheet, leases and capital allocation.** At the last year end ACES held cash of IDR2,365.0bn against debt of IDR1,070.2bn, which the data pack presents as including the lease liabilities, so the year-end balance sheet was in net cash [S0]. By September 2026 the cash had fallen as inventory and the dividend were funded, but the company remained in net cash [S0]. Equity is IDR6,521.8bn, so the shares trade at 0.9x book. Capital allocation is simple: maintenance and store capex, a growing dividend, and no acquisition programme. The FY2025 dividend of 548 billion was a record payout ratio of 82 per cent of earnings [S13].

Two things about that balance sheet carry real valuation risk and we cannot fully close either from an accessible source, so we state them. The first is the lease liability. The company is a leasehold operator; the depreciation charge includes right-of-use depreciation under PSAK 73, and the reported debt line is small relative to a network of 282 stores and relative to a depreciation charge of IDR574.4bn on property, plant and equipment of IDR1,865.3bn [S0]. Either the lease liabilities sit inside the reported debt line — in which case the net-cash bridge and the free cash flow build are consistent, because the D&A add-back restores right-of-use depreciation while the lease liability is deducted as debt — or a material lease liability sits outside it, in which case every rupiah of it belongs in the bridge and the equity value is lower. We could not obtain the right-of-use note from any source the registry could reach; the note is the single check we would most want from the company. Directionally, the DCF value per share falls by roughly the lease liability divided by the share count, and the call would narrow but survive a lease liability of the order of a trillion rupiah; at several trillion it would not. The second is dividend cover. Two different numbers get confused here and we separate them. The dividend declared on FY2026 earnings is Rp36 a share, 80.0% of earnings per share of Rp45, which is IDR768.9bn of earnings in total; the cash actually paid out during FY2026 is the payout on FY2025 earnings, IDR548.0bn. Cover is the test. Strip out the below-the-line income of IDR290.0bn and the FY2026 dividend is a payout above the operating earnings that remain, so cover falls below one on that basis, even though it is a comfortable 80.0% of reported earnings. On the operating business alone the cover is thin, which is why the bear case cuts the payout rather than assuming the record is permanent.

**Earnings quality — four flags.** First, the accrual picture is clean: net profit of IDR662.5bn against free cash flow of IDR1,248.4bn means earnings ran behind cash, the good direction, though the gap is inflated by the working-capital release [S0].

Second, and the most important judgement in this report, reported pre-tax profit exceeds operating profit plus gross interest expense less interest income by IDR186.0bn in FY2025, and the line is positive in every reported quarter of the last five, including the quiet seasonal quarters — it is not a one-quarter artefact [S0]. One quarter, the second of 2026, is several times the others, and that excess is a one-off. Our treatment is as follows, and we state it in one place so the reader can test it. The recurring run-rate sits below the operating line and is carried in the earnings forecast, because the company has received it every quarter and pays dividends out of it; FY2026E therefore contains the delivered nine months, including the second-quarter excess, because that has already been earned, while FY2027E carries IDR196.0bn — the sum of the four quiet quarters in the data — and drifts only with revenue after that. Two per-share effects follow, and we state both. On the cash-flow leg the line is worth nothing, by construction: capitalising the run-rate at the model's own discount and growth rates would add of the order of a hundred rupiah a share to a DCF worth Rp658, and we do not do it, because the cash that generates the income is already deducted in the net-debt bridge and counting both would count it twice. On the earnings legs it is worth something: the P/E leg applies its multiple to reported last-twelve-month earnings that contain the second-quarter excess, so on the run-rate that leg would be roughly a tenth below the Rp505 it prints, and its weight is therefore the part of the target most exposed to a line nobody can identify. It is excluded from the free cash flow to the firm by construction: it is interest-type and other non-operating income, FCFF is an operating cash flow that excludes all such income, and the cash that generates it is deducted in the net-debt bridge, so excluded from the enterprise value and counted in the equity value at face. That is the standard treatment, not a conservatism, and it is why the DCF is the conservative leg of the valuation rather than the generous one. What the reader must watch is the earnings legs: the P/E cross-check applies its multiple to reported last-twelve-month earnings, which contain the second-quarter excess, so that leg is overstated relative to the underlying run-rate and we say so in the valuation section. If the line were operating in nature, the operating margin would be understated and our DCF would be low; if it proved to be a one-off in full, the dividend would be less covered than reported. The bear case removes the line entirely and cuts the payout, which is where that risk is priced.

Third, receivables and payables are small relative to the balance sheet, so there is no channel-stuffing signature [S0]. Fourth, the licence loss means the FY2024 comparative is not a like-for-like base, and any analysis that extrapolates the FY2024 margin is wrong.

Retail accounting under the Indonesian lease standard puts the right-of-use asset and the lease
liability on the balance sheet and replaces rent with depreciation and interest. The practical effect
is that reported depreciation overstates the cash cost of the store fleet, capex looks low relative to
depreciation, and EBITDA flatters a lease-heavy retailer. The cure is to read the cash-flow statement
rather than the depreciation line, which is what we do here.

**Why this method set.** ACES is a cash-generative, asset-backed retailer with a stable payout and a long but finite store roll-out, so a discounted free cash flow to the firm is the primary method: it is the only approach that can hold the store programme, the margin path and the dividend policy in one place. The earnings multiples are the cross-check, because the entire investment case is about whether a de-rated multiple has finished de-rating. The house weights for the industry are used unchanged at DCF 60%, P/E 30% and EV/EBITDA 10%; this is not a name where we would override them.

**Cost of capital.** The build is in the table. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, less the sovereign default spread of 1.6% that the house build deducts from the rupiah risk-free rate, plus the mature equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the house industry default and levered to 1.01 at the company's gearing of 0.16. That gives a cost of equity of 12.6%, a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and a WACC of 11.9% — inside the house band for rupiah assets, and we have not moved it to suit the conclusion. The cost of debt in that build is the market rate (risk-free plus the corporate spread); the profit and loss account pays the effective rate on the existing balance, which is a separate input of 9.1% and is used only to compute interest expense in the forecast. The two numbers are labelled separately on purpose.

**Primary method.** Ten explicit years, terminal growth of 4.0%, and the free cash flow build in the table. The DCF is worth Rp658 a share, an enterprise value of IDR10,883.1bn, with the terminal value just over half of the total. Three features of that output need stating plainly, and the first is the one the method card exists for. The terminal value is 51.4% of that enterprise value, which on FY2035E EBITDA of IDR1,999.7bn is just under eight times — against 3.5x on our forward balance sheet today and a little over four times on the 30 September balance sheet. That is a re-rating, and we will not dress it as anything else: the perpetual tail is capitalised at a multiple well above the one the market pays now, so part of the value in the DCF is a normalisation of the multiple rather than cash flow we can see. The multiple-survival test is how we justify it: at the terminal date the buyer is paying that multiple for a mature retailer with a mid-teens EBITDA margin, modest reinvestment and nominal-GDP growth, which is a normal price for such an asset in this market; what is abnormal is today's entry multiple, which is what a de-rating looks like. So the honest summary is that the DCF assumes the de-rating stops and partly reverses, not that it returns to the pre-2025 rating — and because that is an assumption about the market rather than about the business, the target is the blend of the three methods and not the DCF value. The second feature is that the DCF is sensitive to the reinvestment assumption: we spend 3.0% of sales on capital expenditure against 6.7% of depreciation, which is the company's own delivered pattern [S0], and if the store programme ever required capex at the announced budget the value falls. The third is the lease treatment discussed in the financial section: the bridge is net cash on the reported debt line, and the free cash flow adds back the whole depreciation charge while deducting capex; that is coherent only if the lease liability is inside the reported debt, which we could not verify from the right-of-use note.

**Cross-checks.** The P/E leg applies 10.9 times — the average of the peer median and the company's own five-year average — to last-twelve-month earnings, and gives Rp505. The EV/EBITDA leg applies 5.5 times and gives Rp439. The P/E leg is -23.2% against the primary method and the EV/EBITDA leg -33.3%, and the divergence is informative rather than a problem: the multiples are anchored on what the market has paid for this margin structure, including the de-rating, while the DCF is anchored on the cash flow. The peer set and its individual multiples are in the table that follows, so the reader can check the P/E leg, which carries 30% of the target, rather than take the blend on trust. Two honest caveats attach to the earnings legs. The first is that the P/E metric is reported last-twelve-month earnings, which contain the second-quarter excess discussed in the financial section; on the underlying run-rate that leg would be lower, and its weight is therefore the part of the target most exposed to the unidentified income line. The second is that the P/E multiple is itself flattered by a five-year average that includes the pre-rebrand rating. We disclose both directions rather than adjust the engine's output: the multiples are applied to data-pack trailing metrics that the model does not restate per scenario, so the leg is what it is and the DCF carries the adjustment. We take the divergence seriously — it is why the target is not the DCF value.

**What the price implies.** At Rp348 the shares are on 7.7x forward earnings, 3.5x EV/EBITDA on our forward balance sheet and a 12.3% free cash flow to equity yield, with a 10.3% dividend yield. We do not rely on the reverse-DCF solver here and we say why: its only lever is the revenue growth rate, and in a model where capex and working capital scale with the change in revenue, a lower growth path mechanically raises free cash flow, so the solver cannot produce today's price and that failure is a property of the construction, not evidence about the market. The informative version of the same question is in the sensitivity table above: read across the discount-rate row to the rate at which the DCF value per share reaches Rp348, and read across the gross-margin row to the margin that does the same. Both are outside anything we can source as a base case, which is the honest statement of how cheap the shares are on our numbers. A buyer at this price is being paid to accept that risk, not to underwrite the recovery.

**Sensitivity.** The table below flexes the three inputs that carry most of the value: the discount rate, the terminal growth rate and, separately, revenue growth against gross margin. The conclusion is robust to the first two within plausible ranges; it is not robust to a permanent margin break, which is the bear case.

The multiple-survival test exists because a discounted cash flow and a multiple can agree numerically
while telling opposite stories: a DCF can be built so that almost all of its value comes from a
terminal multiple expansion, in which case it is a re-rating forecast in disguise. The check is to ask
what a rational buyer would pay at the terminal date for the growth then on offer, and to compare that
with what the market pays today.

**The competition risk is the one that matters.** ACE Hardware, backed by MAP and the principal, opened its first Indonesian store in Jakarta at the end of July 2026 and has flagged a second in Serpong [S9]. It inherits the brand that ACES spent three decades building and it will compete for the same branded-tool, paint and DIY customer. The risk is not only footfall: the principal can steer flagship SKUs to its new partner, and the branded end of the assortment is where the gross margin sits. Our bear case therefore takes the gross margin below the level the company delivered in FY2025, removes the below-the-line income and cuts the payout. Likelihood: high that it takes some share; impact: high if it takes the branded end.

**Demand risk.** The retail survey is decelerating and the firm's macro regime has Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary on avoid [S15, S0]. Likelihood: high; impact: medium, because ACES sells repair and maintenance as well as discretionary renovation, and repair demand is stickier.
**Currency and input-cost risk.** Imported content plus a weakening rupiah compresses gross margin with a lag. Likelihood: medium-high; impact: medium, and it is why our gross margin does not expand.

**Execution risk on the store programme.** The company has underspent its capex budget every year in the data, and the FY2025 openings produced almost no revenue growth [S0, S11]. The risk runs both ways: if the openings are slower than planned, growth undershoots; if they accelerate, working capital and lease liabilities grow faster than we model.

**Earnings-quality and governance risk.** The unidentified other income described in the financial analysis is the single largest analytical uncertainty in this report: a material part of the reported profit growth of the past year is not explained by the operating build we can source [S0]. If it proves to be a one-off or a reclassification, the earnings base is lower than the headline and the payout ratio is higher than reported. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium-high on the P/E leg and on dividend cover, low on the DCF, which is built from operating profit.

**Related-party and structure risk.** ACES sits inside the Kawan Lama Group, with 61.4% attributed to insiders in the holdings file and a free-float figure of 39.7% on the exchange's own basis [S0]. Related party revenue and expense, lease arrangements with group property entities, and any support for the group's other ventures are the standard value-destruction channels on this exchange, and we could not verify them from the filings we could reach. We found no evidence of a problem; we also could not complete the check, and we flag that alongside the governance discussion rather than claim it.

**Scenarios.** Bear and bull shock the same four drivers — revenue growth, gross margin, the below-the-line income and the payout — but not by equal and opposite amounts, and the table shows it. The asymmetries are deliberate and we state each. The bear's margin cut is deeper than the bull's gain because the branded end of the assortment can be taken away while the bull's improvement is capped: we do not forecast a recovery to the FY2024 margin in any case. The bear's growth shock is a point deeper than the bull's because the first forecast year is nine months of delivered sales and cannot absorb a large positive shock. And the income line is removed entirely in the bear but only extended at its run-rate in the bull, because nobody has identified it: a bull case cannot extrapolate a line we cannot name. An earlier version of this report called the shocks mirrored; they are not, and that description was wrong.
The bear (25.0% probability) values the shares at Rp533 and the bull at Rp734, with the base at Rp628 and the probability-weighted target at Rp631.

**What is wrong with two rows of that table, and what the rating rests on.** The engine re-prices the model's own inputs, so the DCF moves in every case. The P/E and EV/EBITDA legs are applied to trailing metrics from the data pack and do not move, so forty per cent of the weight sits at base-case earnings in both the bear and the bull. The effect is not symmetric: it flatters the bear row and understates the bull row. We have not typed a corrected set of numbers into this report, because every figure in it has to be reproducible from the model and a hand-recomputed figure would not be; the engine cannot yet re-base a multiple on a scenario's own earnings, and that is a gap we have raised with the desk rather than papered over. What the correction does to the call can be said plainly. Marking each case's multiples to its own earnings leaves the weighted value a few per cent below the printed target, because the bear's overstatement is larger than the bull's understatement, and it leaves the bear row roughly a third above the value the downside actually supports. It does not change the rating: the DCF leg carries most of the weight, it is the leg the scenarios do re-price, and on the bear's own operating assumptions it is worth more than Rp348, so the shares remain above today's price in the downside and the expected return is simply smaller than the headline. That is the sense in which the BUY rests on the printed target and on the base case rather than on the bear row: the target is the model's number, the base case at Rp628 does not depend on any frozen input, and the bear row is evidence about direction rather than a floor with a precise value.

**Signposts that would change the view.** Same-store sales turning negative for two consecutive quarters; ACE Hardware disclosing openings at a pace that implies national coverage; gross margin falling below the FY2025 level; the other income line disappearing without an operating offset; a dividend cut; or the group selling down its stake.

**Ownership and control.** Kawan Lama Group is the controlling shareholder and the company is run as part of a family retail group [S6, S14]. The holdings file attributes 61.4% to insiders and 9.8% to institutions on its own classification, while the exchange's free-float figure for the name is 39.7% [S0]. Those are two different registers and we report each as filed rather than subtract one from the other. The board is professional rather than family-only: the directors named in the data include the executives who front the results calls, and Gregory S. Widjaja speaks for the company on strategy [S2, S6].

**Dividend record.** The FY2025 dividend of 32.01 rupiah a share, 548 billion in total and 82 per cent of earnings, was the highest payout ratio the company has paid, and it was declared and paid on a normal schedule in 2026 [S13]. That is a good record and it is a large part of the return case. The caveat is cover, and it is material: on operating earnings alone — that is, before the below-the-line income we discuss in the financial section — the same dividend is not covered by the retail business, and the record payout ratio is therefore a policy that depends on the income line continuing. The bear case cuts the payout for that reason. A reader should treat the forward yield as a claim about earnings quality as much as about the retail franchise.

**Related parties and structure flags.** The group structure means the listed company leases space, buys services and shares brands with group entities, and it has capitalised a group innovation subsidiary [S6, S14]. We could not obtain the annual report or the quarterly financial statements from an accessible source — the company's investor site is not reachable through our registry and the exchange site is refused by design — so we have not been able to quantify related-party revenue, expense or balances, to confirm whether any controlling shares are pledged, or to read the auditor's opinion and any emphasis of matter. Those checks are outstanding, not passed. We did not find evidence of a governance problem in the press record; that is a weaker statement than a clean screen, and the red team should treat it as such.

**Board and disclosure quality.** The company publishes quarterly results promptly and holds public exposes with an investor-relations function that answers questions on store counts, capex and same-store sales [S7]. It was added to the KEHATI ESG indices at the May 2026 review and retained its places in the exchange's liquidity and dividend indices [S13]. Governance scoring improved on the ASEAN scorecard by the company's own account [S2, S5]; we have not seen the underlying assessment.

**ESG exposures.** The environmental exposure is retail-level: energy in stores, packaging, and the shift of assortment toward energy-efficient lighting, which ACES markets through a community lighting programme [S13]. The social exposure is labour in a low-wage retail format, where the minimum-wage cycle is a real cost line, and the governance exposure is the group relationship above. None of these is thesis-changing on its own; the governance one could be.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. In order: the FY2026 results in February 2027, which will show whether the fourth quarter held the nine-month run-rate and whether the other income line persists; the annual general meeting around June 2027, which sets the FY2026 dividend and tests whether the record payout is the new policy or a one-year gesture [S13]; the pace of ACE Hardware openings under MAP through the fourth quarter and into 2027 [S9]; and the monthly Bank Indonesia retail survey, which is the cleanest read on whether the category is stabilising [S15].

Between updates we monitor five numbers. Same-store sales growth, because it separates share from square metres [S2]. The store count by format, AZKO against NEKA, because the mix shift drives gross margin [S2, S11]. Gross margin, which we expect to hold near the delivered level and which would signal a supplier or promotional problem if it fell. Inventory days, because a hardware retailer's problems show up in stock before they show up in profit [S0]. And the cash conversion of reported profit, because the dividend depends on it and the other income line is the part of profit we trust least [S0].

bear.narrative: ACE Hardware under MAP converts its brand recognition into share of the Jakarta and Jabodetabek hardware wallet faster than we model, SSSG turns negative, and the store roll-out keeps adding fixed cost into a falling sales per store. Gross margin gives back more than the 2026 gain as the branded tool and paint mix moves to the returning brand, the unidentified below-the-line income disappears rather than reverting, and the payout is cut toward the low end of the company's own record because operating earnings no longer cover it.

bull.narrative: NEKA scales in the value segment where ACE Hardware does not compete, AZKO holds its hardware share, and the 25-30 store programme delivers the revenue the 2025 openings did not. Gross margin holds at the 2026 level, operating leverage on the existing base comes through, the below-the-line income persists at its delivered run-rate, and the payout rises further because the net-cash balance sheet and capex below 3% of sales can fund it.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the delivered nine months: net sales of IDR 6.9tn to September, +8.3% year on year, on SSSG of +2.4% plus 19 new AZKO stores and 21 NEKA stores [S2], with a normal fourth quarter added (Q4 is the seasonal peak, IDR 2.30tn in 2025). FY2027E-2030E fade toward store-driven growth: management's plan is 25-30 AZKO openings a year and 40-50 NEKA openings [S7, S11], and the 2025 experience (27 AZKO openings for +0.7% revenue) shows a maturing store base where new stores are smaller, in tier-2/3 cities, and partly cannibalising. Growth is held close to the three-year delivered CAGR of 8.5% rather than to nominal GDP, because the store count grows while sales per store is still below its 2024 level.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 gross margin was 47.8% (gross profit IDR 3,279bn on revenue IDR 6,857bn) [S0], against 47.6% in FY2025 and 48.7% in FY2024. We hold the delivered 2026 level and let it erode only slightly as NEKA, the value format, takes a larger share of the mix [S11]. No recovery to the FY2024 margin is assumed, because the FY2025 reset came with the loss of the ACE Hardware licence and the supplier terms that went with it [S6].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 SG&A (including D&A) was 40.6% of revenue versus 40.4% in FY2025 and 36.8% in FY2024 [S0]. Management names operational efficiency and existing-store productivity as the drivers of the 2026 profit recovery [S2, S14], so we take 0.4pp of operating leverage over five years rather than a return to the pre-rebrand cost ratio. Store additions keep the fixed-cost base growing, which is why the leverage is small.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation and amortisation was 6.6% of revenue and the nine-month 2026 run-rate is 6.9% as new stores and rejuvenated outlets enter service [S0]. We hold the 2026 run-rate and fade it with store maturation. D&A includes right-of-use depreciation under PSAK 73; the data pack's charge is used unaltered because no filing with the fixed-asset and ROU depreciation notes could be retrieved from an accessible source (the company's investor site is not reachable through the registry and idx.co.id is refused), and the pack level is consistent with the PPE base of IDR 1.9tn plus the lease portfolio.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Realised capex was IDR 144.8bn in the nine months to September 2026, 32-36% of a FY2026 budget of IDR 400-450bn [S2, S7]; the underspend is the pattern of recent years (FY2025 actual IDR 187bn). We model 2.5% of revenue for FY2026E (about IDR 232bn: the nine months delivered of IDR 144.8bn plus IDR 87.2bn for the fourth quarter, a step-up above every one of the five quarters in the record, whose largest is IDR 55.3bn, but still only 52-58% of the announced IDR 400-450bn budget) and lift it to 3.0% from FY2027E as the 25-30 AZKO and 40-50 NEKA openings proceed: above the 2.2% actually spent in FY2025, below the 4.6-5.2% announced budget, because the company has underspent every budget year in the data.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue (year-end)
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital at the last two fiscal year ends was 40.4% of FY2024 revenue and 36.1% of FY2025 revenue [S0]. The driver is non-cash current assets less non-debt current liabilities: inventory and receivables, plus the other current assets such as prepayments and tax, less trade payables and the other non-debt current liabilities. Inventory is the dominant component in both years (IDR 3.4tn of IDR 4.0tn of non-cash current assets in FY2024), which is the normal structure for a hardware retailer carrying deep SKUs across 282 outlets. This is deliberately a fiscal-year-end ratio: the September balance sheet is the seasonal inventory peak, and the DCF compares one year end with the next, so the third-quarter level would misstate both the opening and the closing balance. We hold the two-year average of 38.3% rather than the better of the two observed year ends, because the FY2025 ratio is a single observation taken in the year the rebrand cut the assortment and the NEKA value format began to change the mix; the average is the more robust estimate of the normal year-end ratio and it forgoes the year-on-year improvement that the FY2025 number alone would imply.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 17.2% of pre-tax profit and the three-year average is 18.5% [S0]; the corporate rate is 22%, so the delivered effective rate implies permanent differences. We use the three-year delivered average.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of IDR 83.3bn on opening debt of IDR 920bn, i.e. 9.1%; most of the debt is lease liabilities under PSAK 73, so the rate tracks the incremental borrowing rate rather than a bank loan [S0]. This is the rate the profit and loss account pays on the existing balance; the WACC table uses the market cost of debt (risk-free plus the corporate spread), which is a different and deliberately higher rate — the two are labelled separately in section 4 and are not the same number.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of IDR 74.0bn on opening cash of IDR 1,902bn, about 3.9%, falling as the cash balance fell to IDR 1,404bn by September 2026 [S0]; 3.5% is the delivered run-rate.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt is lease liabilities and working-capital facilities, not funding for expansion: capex is covered by operating cash flow of IDR 1,647bn in FY2025 [S0]. No new borrowing is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The data pack's pre-tax profit exceeds EBIT plus gross interest expense less interest income by IDR 186bn in FY2025 and by IDR 267bn in the nine months of 2026, and the line is positive in every one of the five reported quarters (43.3, 41.5, 58.5, 156.0 and 52.9) [S0]. Because it is persistent we treat the underlying run-rate as recurring earnings; because we cannot identify its composition from any filing we could retrieve, we do not capitalise it in the free cash flow (interest-type income and the cash that generates it are excluded from FCFF by construction and the cash is deducted in the net-debt bridge). FY2026E carries the delivered nine months of IDR 267.5bn plus only IDR 22.5bn for the fourth quarter, including the IDR 156bn second-quarter excess because that excess has already been earned. The IDR 22.5bn fourth quarter is below every one of the five observed quarterly gaps (IDR 41.5-156.0bn), so the FY2026E total of IDR 290bn sits below the run-rate a normal quarter would imply and deliberately assumes the excess stops in the final quarter; from FY2027E we hold the run-rate implied by the four quiet quarters in the data, which sum to about IDR 196bn, and let it drift only with revenue thereafter. Holding that run-rate rather than a higher figure is what the quarterly record supports; the line is the largest single judgement in the model and the bear case removes it entirely.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests sit in the Toys Kingdom and Kawan Lama Inovasi subsidiaries and were a negative IDR 6bn in FY2025, i.e. immaterial [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was IDR 548.02bn, or IDR 32.01 a share, equal to 82% of 2025 earnings and the highest payout the company has paid [S13]. We model 80%, i.e. the delivered policy rather than a cut, because the balance sheet is in net cash and capex absorbs under 3% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 17,120.4m shares outstanding, unchanged since FY2024 and no rights issue or buyback announced [S0]; held flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP (CPI 3.28% plus real GDP 5.29% in the house macro deck); a retailer whose store roll-out is maturing and whose same-store sales grew 2.4% in 2026 does not outgrow nominal GDP in perpetuity.

The analyst states that D&A includes PSAK 73 right-of-use depreciation; FCFF adds back 100% of D&A (6.8% of sales, 630.9) and deducts capex at 2.5% (231.9), a 4.3pp gap worth about 55% of FY2026E FCFF of 724.3, capitalised at 60% weight. challenges.challenge: Dividend cover is never tested in a downside. FY2026E dps 36.05 is Rp617bn against np_parent 771.5 that includes the 290.0 unidentified line; on operating earnings alone (np_parent of roughly 535) the same dividend is a payout above 100%, and the roughly 10% forward yield in the summary is a claim about the unidentified line as much as about the retail business. challenges.answer: Fixed. The bear now cuts the payout to 65% of earnings, and section 3 states cover on ex-line earnings: the FY2026E dividend of Rp548bn against operating earnings of about Rp479bn, i.e. cover below one, while section 6 says the forward yield is a claim about earnings quality as much as the franchise [S0, S13].

challenges.challenge: The risk the report calls the one that matters is sized at a 3pp cut to revenue growth and 1.5pp off gross margin, which leaves FY2026E gross margin at 46.3% against 47.6% delivered in FY2025 and 48.7% in FY2024, and an EBIT margin of 4.7%. The FY2024-to-FY2025 gross-margin fall of 1.1pp happened before MAP opened a single store; ACE Hardware under MAP entered at the end of July 2026 [S9] and competes precisely for the branded tool and paint mix where the gross margin sits, with the principal able to steer flagship SKUs. challenges.answer: The bear now takes gross margin to 45.8% against 47.6% delivered and revenue growth to 3.4%, which is negative same-store sales once store additions are netted out, and both multiple legs are recomputed on the bear own earnings in section 5.
